Central Nervous System
Histology
Ganglia, Synapse, Nerve ending

This lesson covers three peripheral components of the nervous system. Ganglia are peripheral clusters of nerve cell bodies, divided into sensory and autonomic types. Synapses are the sites of impulse transmission between neurons and other cells, and nerve endings are the receptors and effectors at the periphery. Together they show how impulses enter and leave the nervous system.

Ganglia

Definition: ovoid structures formed by an aggregation of nerve cell bodies and glial cells, supported by connective tissue and located outside the CNS.

There are two types: sensory (spinal) ganglia and autonomic ganglia (sympathetic and parasympathetic).

Sensory ganglia

  • Related to peripheral nerves: cranial ganglia (cranial nerves) and spinal (dorsal root) ganglia (spinal nerves).
  • Covered by a thick connective tissue capsule.
  • Contain pseudounipolar neurons: a single process divides into a peripheral process (acts as a dendrite) and a central process that enters the spinal cord as an axon. Both have the structure of an axon.
  • Cells are rounded, large and variable in size, arranged in groups, with a large central nucleus and prominent nucleoli.
  • Surrounded by small, numerous glial satellite cells; myelinated nerve fibers lie between the nerve cells.
  • No synapses are present inside spinal ganglia.
  • Function: receive sensory impulses from different parts of the body and transmit them to the CNS. Impulses pass from the peripheral process to the central process without passing through the nerve cell body.

Autonomic (sympathetic) ganglia

  • Found in the sympathetic chain adjacent to the spinal cord, within certain organs, or along the abdominal aorta.
  • Covered by a thin connective tissue capsule.
  • Nerve cells are multipolar: small and branched, with rounded, pale, eccentric nuclei. Cells are nearly equal in size and surrounded by few satellite cells.
  • Nerve fibers are either myelinated or unmyelinated.
  • Motor in function: preganglionic fibers synapse with the ganglion cells, whose axons leave the ganglion as postganglionic fibers.

Sensory versus autonomic ganglia

FeatureSensory gangliaAutonomic ganglia
Types and siteCranial ganglia; spinal gangliaSympathetic ganglia; parasympathetic ganglia
FunctionSensoryMotor
CapsuleThick and poorly vascularThin and vascular
Nerve cellsPseudounipolar; large and variable in size; arranged in groups; nucleus large, spherical, central; satellite cells numerousMultipolar; small and equal in size; distributed throughout the ganglion; nucleus rounded, vesicular, eccentric; satellite cells few
Nerve fibersThick and myelinated; widely separated from each otherThin, non-myelinated and myelinated; close to each other
SynapsesNonePresent

Synapses

Synapses are the sites where nerve impulses are transmitted from one neuron to another cell: a neuron, a myocyte or glandular tissue.

Classification

By site of synaptic contact

  • Axo-dendritic: between an axon and a dendrite.
  • Axo-somatic: between an axon and a soma.
  • Axo-axonic: between two axons.

By mode of transmission

  • Electrical synapse: movement of ions from one neuron to another via gap junctions.
  • Chemical synapse: release of a chemical substance (neurotransmitter), e.g. acetylcholine.

Structure of a chemical synapse

  1. Axon terminal: contains many mitochondria, few SER and synaptic vesicles that hold the neurotransmitters.
  2. Presynaptic membrane: the axolemma of the terminal bulb; thick and electron dense.
  3. Synaptic cleft: a gap about 20 nm wide between the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes.
  4. Postsynaptic membrane: the thickened plasma membrane of the neuron or other target cell (e.g. muscle) receiving the impulse; it has specific receptors for the neurotransmitters.

Nerve endings

Nerve endings are special nervous structures that include receptors and effectors.

Receptors

Non-encapsulated: free nerve endings, peritrichial nerve endings, Merkel's disc.

Encapsulated: Meissner's corpuscles, Ruffini corpuscles, Krause end bulbs, Pacinian corpuscles, muscle spindle (and the tendon spindle of Golgi, a proprioceptor in tendons and joints).

ReceptorSitesStructureFunction
Free nerve endings (non-encapsulated)Epidermis of skin, cornea, oral cavity, connective tissueNerve loses its myelin just beneath the epidermis and branches among epidermal cells, ending between the cellsPain and temperature
Merkel's discs (non-encapsulated)Epidermis of soles, palms, fingertips, lipsUnmyelinated fiber enters between epithelial cells and ends as an expanded disc under Merkel's cells in the basal layersTouch
Peritrichial endings (non-encapsulated)Around hair folliclesUnmyelinated fibers surround the base and shaft of the follicleTouch and hair movement
Meissner's corpusclesDermal papillae of palms, soles, lips, external genitalia, nipples, eyelidsPear-shaped, connective tissue capsule; unmyelinated nerve enters the lower pole and follows a spiral or zigzag course among flattened transverse cells (modified Schwann cells or fibroblasts)Touch; tactile discrimination
Krause end bulbsPapillary dermis; mucous membrane of external genitalia, tongue, mouth, conjunctivaSpherical, thin capsule; myelinated fiber loses its myelin and branches into unmyelinated fibers with expanded endsDeep pressure and touch
Ruffini corpusclesDermis and hypodermis, nail beds, joint capsulesFusiform (1 mm × 0.2 mm), thin capsule, parallel to the skin surface; nerve loses myelin and ends in terminal swellings; collagen bundles run between the fibersMechanoreceptors for stretch and pressure in skin and joint capsule
Pacinian corpusclesDermis and hypodermis (palm, sole, fingertips, breast, external genitalia); connective tissue of joints, mesentery, tendons, ligaments, pancreas, skeletal muscleOnion-like, oval (1–2 mm × 0.5 mm), thin capsule; nerve enters at one end, loses myelin and runs the whole length to an expanded terminal; surrounded by 20–60 concentric lamellae of flat modified fibroblasts separated by fluidPressure, touch and vibration (acts as a proprioceptor)

The muscle spindle is a muscle proprioceptor responding to the state of the muscle and to muscle stretch. The tendon spindle of Golgi is a proprioceptor present in tendons and joints.

Effectors

  • Motor end plate: a specialized junctional zone between a terminal motor nerve fiber and the muscle fiber it supplies.
  • Autonomic nerve endings: terminal fibers generally show swellings associated with the effector cells (gland or smooth muscle cells) but separated from them by a synaptic cleft. Numerous synaptic vesicles are present: norepinephrine at sympathetic endings and acetylcholine at parasympathetic endings.

Key Points / Quick Review

Sensory ganglia

  • Cranial and dorsal root; thick capsule.
  • Pseudounipolar cells, numerous satellite cells, no synapses.
  • Impulse bypasses the cell body.

Autonomic ganglia

  • Multipolar, small, eccentric nuclei, few satellite cells.
  • Thin vascular capsule; synapses present; motor.
  • Preganglionic synapses give rise to postganglionic fibers.

Synapse

  • Axo-dendritic, axo-somatic, axo-axonic.
  • Electrical (gap junctions) or chemical (neurotransmitter).
  • Presynaptic membrane, 20 nm cleft, postsynaptic membrane with receptors.

Non-encapsulated receptors

  • Free endings: pain, temperature.
  • Merkel's discs: touch.
  • Peritrichial: touch, hair movement.

Encapsulated receptors

  • Meissner: tactile discrimination.
  • Krause: deep pressure and touch.
  • Ruffini: stretch and pressure.
  • Pacinian: pressure, touch, vibration.

Effectors

  • Motor end plate on skeletal muscle.
  • Autonomic swellings: norepinephrine (sympathetic), acetylcholine (parasympathetic).
